A 46-year-old woman complained of lower back pain,
progressive tightness, and painful spasm of muscles of both
legs and abdomen for the last 3 years. On examination, she
had profound lumbar lordosis, extreme painful stiffness of
the abdominal wall, increased muscle tone in the left leg,
brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Trömner and Hoffmann
signs, and flexor plantar responses. Cerebellar function
examination disclosed mild right-sided limb dysmetria and
dysdiadochokinesis. The gait was slow, wide-based, and
unsteady. Needle electromyography revealed continuous
motor unit activity of rectus abdominis and paraspinal
muscles at rest, which was completely abolished after
10 mg of intravenous diazepam. A shortened silent period
was recorded from all four extremities after transcranial
magnetic stimulation. A meticulous laboratory work-up
disclosed pernicious anemia, family history of IDDM, and
the presence of HLA alleles DQB1 0201 and DRB1 0301.
Serum titer of GAD-Abs was markedly increased (81,858 U/
ml; normal <1000). The various forms of hereditary cerebel-
lar ataxia were ruled out by the appropriate molecular
genetic tests. Anti-Yo and anti-Hu antibodies were negative
and brain MRI was normal. During 1 year of follow-up and
prior to the present recording of ocular movements, there
was a modest benefit from intravenous immunoglobulins
and a much more significant benefit from daily oral
diazepam. However, a progressive impairment of eye move-
ments was documented. Initially, the range of voluntary eye
movements was full in all directions, but horizontal and
vertical saccades were slow. It also seemed that smooth
pursuit and vestibulo-ocular reflexes were normal. On a
follow-up visit 6 months later, she complained of positional
vertigo, and on examination, downbeating nystagmus was
present when she was lying down; this was most prominent
on left gaze.
4.2. Eye movement recordings and data analysis
The experimental paradigms and data collection were done
using Labview (National Instrument), and analysis of the
data was performed using Matlab. Horizontal and vertical
gaze of the right eye and head rotations were measured
using the magnetic search coil technique ( Robinson, 1963 )
with 6-ft field coils (CNC Engineering, Seattle, WA) using a
scleral search coil embedded in a silastic ring (Skalar, Delft,
Netherlands). The eye movement recordings were monocu-
lar because clinically all eye movements appeared to be
conjugate, and there was no clinical complaint of diplopia.
The coils were pre-calibrated using a protractor device. The
coil was placed on the eye after application of two drops of
local anesthetic (benoxinate HCl 0.4%). Coil signals were
filtered (bandwidth 0 –200 Hz) prior to digitization at 500 Hz
sampling rate, with 12-bit resolution. The visual stimulus
was a red laser spot (1.5 mm diameter) rear-projected onto
a semitranslucent screen situated 1.1 m in front of the
subject. The position of the laser spot was determined by
an X –Y galvanometer. The subject sat in front of the screen
in a dark room and was given time to adjust to the dark.
Her head was immobilized with a head restraint device
attached to the chair. Smooth pursuit eye movements were
tested by having the subject track a target moving at 10°/s
from eccentric (between 7.5 and 15°) positions to the origin.
Saccades were tested by having the target step right, left,

up, or down along one of the principal axes between 5 and
15°. VOR was measured by rotating the chair in a sinusoidal
manner back and forth at approximately 0.4 Hz. In addition,
the response to head thrusts was measured by asking the
patient to fixate her gaze on the laser spot target, while her
head was held from behind by one of the investigators who
executed sudden, rapid, unpredictable angular head rota-
tions to both sides.
Direct current electro-oculgraphic (EOG) recording was
performed to measure positional downbeating nystagmus
and vestibular response to standard caloric stimulation. The
EOG was utilized for these two tests because the coil system is
not set up for use with a supine subject.
